title: CSV Lat/Lng Validator: Plot-Ready Columns
description: Validate spreadsheet lat/lng columns before plotting or geocoding with the CSV Lat/Lng Validator — quick pair checks for map-bound files. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 200-row event file with three rows whose latitude and longitude traded places gets flagged before the plot scatters those events across the southern ocean.
quick_answer: The CSV Lat/Lng Validator validates spreadsheet coordinate columns before you plot them or spend geocoding effort. Paste the CSV and check each lat/lng pair for presence, numeric form and sane ranges — the fast pre-flight that keeps spreadsheet geography honest on its way to a map.

Rows whose pairs already validate need no geocoder. The validator sorts the file into ‘already located’ and ‘needs work’ before a single API credit burns.
Files many hands edit accumulate creative coordinate formats. A validation pass after each workshop keeps the master sheet plot-ready.
Class projects and community surveys enter coordinates by hand — enthusiasm high, formatting wild. Validation is the kind gatekeeper.

body.t: Chicago written as lat −87.63, lon 41.88 is range-legal and geographically absurd (Antarctic waters). Pair validators catch form; the plot — or the
— catches swaps. Know which gate you are standing at.
‘41.52.30’ typed from a GPS display is not a decimal and not valid input — it is degrees-minutes-seconds in disguise. Convert the column’s dress first (the coordinate converters), then validate.

popular_table.note: This validator judges pairs as they will be plotted: latitude first-class, longitude first-class, both numeric and in range. What it cannot judge is whether the pair is the right place — that is source-checking.

faq: How is this different from the CSV Coordinate Validator?

Same family, different doorway: that page audits whole-file structure (columns, content classes); this one is the quick pair-focused pre-flight before plotting or geocoding. Files usually meet this one first.
Latitude and longitude columns are identified by their headers — order in the file does not matter, naming does. Rename exotic headers in your pasted copy.
Plus codes or DMS in the columns?
Not decimal pairs — the validator will fail them as non-numeric, correctly. Convert those formats to decimals with the site’s converters first.
Latitude −90…90, longitude −180…180, both present and numeric. Beyond ranges, sanity is context (a Kansas file plotting in Kazakhstan is valid and wrong).
Validation is the gate, plotting is the destination — CSV to Map draws the survivors. Keeping the gates separate is what makes each trustworthy.
Rows with addresses but no pairs?
They fail as unlocated — and they are exactly the geocoding queue. The validator’s failure list doubles as the work list.
Rare in spreadsheets, parseable where valid — 4.07e1 is 40.7. If your export writes coordinates that way, the export settings deserve the fix.
